::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## Status: design. Frame counted. The scoring instrument is the obstacle. Not a protocol.

The frame is large: **630 tier A records and 685 frame records declare a cross-sectional or
methodological design**, of which 67 and 197 respectively name a reporting guideline.

What blocks this from being a protocol is not data but measurement: scoring adherence to STROBE
means reading 22 items per article, and no validated automatic scorer exists. Section 5 is
honest that this is the most expensive study of the set per unit of evidence.
:::

## 1. The question

Meta-research grades other people's papers against reporting checklists. Most meta-research is
itself a cross-sectional study of a sample of articles, and cross-sectional studies have a
checklist: STROBE. A field that measures adherence and does not meet it is making an argument
against its own instrument.

## 2. Hypothesis

Meta-research articles that themselves assess guideline adherence report their own methods more
completely than meta-research articles that do not.

The hypothesis is deliberately internal rather than a comparison against non-meta-research,
because a comparison across fields would confound topic with venue with design. This is the
same structure as [P01v2](P01v2-advocacy-and-practice-protocol.qmd), and the same criticism
applies to it.

**Primary null.** Adherence does not differ by whether the article's own subject is reporting
quality.

**What would falsify it.** No difference, or worse adherence among the auditors.

## 3. Sample

Articles from the tier A corpus and the tier B frame whose design is cross-sectional or
methodological, with PMC full text.

| frame | declaring such a design | naming a reporting guideline |
|---|---|---|
| tier A | 630 | 67 |
| tier B frame | 685 | 197 |

Design is determined from the full text methods section, not from the abstract regex used for
this count. The regex is a frame estimate and is labeled as one.

## 4. Exposure

Whether the article's own subject is reporting quality, from the `report` topic label.

## 5. Outcome, and why this is expensive

A STROBE-based adherence score over the items that apply to a study of documents rather than of
people. Not all 22 items apply; the applicable subset is fixed in advance and published with
the protocol, because choosing which items apply after scoring is how an adherence study
manufactures its own result.

**Scoring requires reading.** The realistic options are:

1. The author scores a random sample of 150 articles. Precise, and the ceiling on sample size.
2. Models score all of them after being validated against the author's 150, gated at kappa 0.70
   per item group, with items that fail the gate dropped and reported as dropped.

Option 2 is the design, with option 1 as its reference standard, and neither can start until
the author's 150 exist.

## 6. Analysis

In R. Linear regression of the adherence proportion on the exposure, adjusted for year and with
journal as a random intercept; and a per-item logistic model so that a difference driven by one
item is visible rather than averaged away.

## 7. Threats, and what happened to each

| threat | what was done | removed or disclosed |
|---|---|---|
| Which STROBE items apply is a choice | Fixed and published before scoring | Removed |
| Scoring by model | Gated against the author's labels per item group; failing items dropped and reported | Disclosed |
| Design determined by regex | Only for the frame count; the analysis reads the methods section | Removed |
| STROBE was not written for studies of documents | True, and the item subset is an interpretation the protocol publishes so it can be disagreed with | Disclosed |
| Reporting completeness is not study quality | Stated; the outcome is what is written, never whether it was done | Disclosed |
| Same structural criticism as P01v2 | The exposure is a vocabulary label and the comparison is internal | Disclosed |

## 8. Probes

| probe | computes | goes to | what would change the design | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **PA** | frame size by declared design | 3 | fewer than about 300 eligible articles makes per-item analysis unusable | done: 630 and 685 |
| **PB** | how many have a methods section PMC structures well enough to score | 3, 5 | poor structure makes automatic scoring impossible and forces option 1 | outstanding |
| **PC** | the applicable STROBE item subset, fixed by the author | 5 | this is a design decision, not a measurement | outstanding, needs the author |
| **PD** | per-item scorer agreement against 150 author-scored articles | 5 | items below kappa 0.70 are dropped | outstanding, needs the author |

## Deviations

Recorded on the result page: what changed, when, why, and the estimate before and after where
that can be computed. A deviation is not a failure; concealing one is.

## What this cannot show

- Reporting completeness is not methodological quality and the study never claims it is.
- A well-reported study can be wrong, and a badly reported one right.
